Whole-repository assessment · 7 September 2026

city-digital-twin, assessed at 419b0da

An agent-based microsimulation of Newcastle, New South Wales — twelve modes, each physically simulated on the real roads and timetables and scored against its own real-life ridership. This is a reading of one commit: every area of the code, every pull request, every run on disk, and the project placed against 41 comparable efforts and 12 platforms.

the one-paragraph verdict

A well-governed instrument that has not yet produced a result

This project is built to a standard its field does not generally attempt. Twelve modes are each scored on their own declared basis; 471 registry fields carry units, provenance and a sweep; 512 manifest rows carry a hash, a producing script and a licence; and a CI-gated check keeps values decided in code at zero. Against 41 surveyed projects it aims at a validation rung — per-mode ridership for every simulated mode — that no other project occupies. But it has not reached it: the current reading comes from an aborted run at its iteration-100 gate, one mode of twelve is inside 10 %, seven are past the 20 % stop bar, and no run since family F4 on 21 August has executed the horizon it declared — the maximum reached_iteration across all 153 run directories is 100. The good news of this pass is that cost is no longer the obstacle: the ride-pairing listener that consumed 56 % of an iteration in F23 now costs 0.8 %, and a 250-iteration arm fits in 18–19 hours where it once needed 44. What the pass finds instead is a governance gap between what the checks assert and what they can see — a holdout breach in the count targets that the artefact itself prints, a hardcoding scanner that reads only module-level ALL-CAPS names, a doc gate that misses one of the two PR paths, and four living documents naming four different packages on disk. None of these would fail a build. Every one of them can send a 22-hour arm after the wrong thing.

The twelve-mode scoreboard, which is the whole point of the project

method

What was read, by whom, and what the ratings mean

Nine phases. Phase 1 collected the mechanical half with three scripts so that no figure in this report is typed by hand. Phases 2–7 then ran as six agents, one per phase — one code reviewer for all six areas, one performance analyst, one historian, one document reviewer, one field researcher, one factor researcher. Two agents were never given the same phase: the previous pass ran three field lanes and three factor lanes in parallel, exhausted its search budget on duplicated queries, and delivered no platform table and not one literature cell.

The rating rubric

Each area carries five scores, 1–5, and each cell names its two strongest pieces of evidence — one for, one against. Ratings are never averaged across areas: a 2 in the build layer and a 4 in the harness describe different risks and do not combine into a 3.

  • 1 — a defect class is live and unguarded.
  • 2 — works, but a known failure mode has no guard.
  • 3 — sound with named exceptions.
  • 4 — the exceptions are documented and tested.
  • 5 — a reader cannot find a way to break it.
On honest partial reads

Where an area was too large to read whole, the reviewer read the ranked subset and declared the blind spot. The Java area was read at 5 %: its ten findings are carried forward on file-identity evidence — the files are byte-identical since bdd40f3 — not on a re-read, and each such row says so. A named blind spot is the deliverable; a silent partial read would be a defect in this report.

30 sessions in 28 days — 7.5 a week — across 23 distinct record dates, producing 115 record sections. The busiest single day, 2026-08-30, carried 31 of them.

What happened, in twelve lines

  1. 10 August - the repository opens with one commit called 'proposal' and, within nine hours, three merged pull requests: P1's 182-file hashed data package, P2's 157,678-link MATSim network with all 15 GTFS feeds mapped, and P3's tour-based demand. None of it had been run, and all three PRs say so.
  2. 11 August - the first attempt to execute MATSim refuses to load all thirty assembled run-input sets. PR #4 fixes three defects, measures the first cost curve (9.8 / 29.9 / ~64 s an iteration) and records that thirteen of the sixty-seven calibration targets can identify nothing.
  3. 15-16 August - PR #38's rebuild: a typed-in OSM harvest box had clipped 87 core SA1s out of the road network. Core SA1s without a road node fall 99 to 4, the config is emitted from 297 declared registry fields, and family F1 produces the project's first completed 1000-iteration arm.
  4. 18-21 August - ride pairing is built and immediately measured starved (0.104% of ride trips share an OD with a household car trip); escort binding and census age structure repair the demand; every person-transport mode becomes physical (F3); the walk wedge is found and repaired (F4) - the last family to date whose arms ran to their declared horizon.
  5. 20-21 August - process hardens after five of six stacked pull requests never reach main: PRs target main only, direct commits to main are banned, and the session's one PR opens at /handoff. The sixth and last direct commit lands seventeen minutes before the rule merges; there has not been one since.
  6. 24-25 August - SUMO is descoped by recorded decision, the signals run stack is pinned by sha256, and the all-modes batch (signals, taxi, crossings, dwell) is built inert with byte-identical run inputs, then activated as family F6. The first gate stop follows the same day.
  7. 25 August - two documentation PRs answer the drift the front door had accumulated: check_doc_currency.py pins every live-state number to its artefact (#83), and the light rail's published -63% 'error' is retracted against a target the fit itself marks unscorable (#85).
  8. 27-29 August - the gate loop starts firing on the twenty-percent bar. PR #95 fixes three yardsticks that had been wrong at every iteration - one counted another city's light rail stop - and corrects four of its own session's conclusions in the same body.
  9. 30 August - the busiest day of the project: 87 commits, six comparability families (F15-F20), 31 record sections, a demand rebuilt twice, and the document restructure into GOAL.md, a one-page generated board and thirteen position pages, so a session reads 600 lines instead of a 13,000-line record.
  10. 31 August - 2 September - public transport is priced at the published Opal fare, then bike stress, parking search time and income-scaled money sensitivity enter the model. Bus comes inside its band at the F22 gate, the first of the twelve modes ever to; the results store makes the run lifecycle automatic.
  11. 3-5 September - the first whole-repository assessment lodges 26 issues and the next PR closes fourteen of them without a run, correcting seven of the report's own proposed fixes first. Destination choice is constrained at both ends, the iteration is profiled (60% in one before-mobsim listener) and cut, and F25 falsifies the demand-side explanation for the ride deficit.
  12. 6-7 September - a declared ride driver must own a car (F26); a global qsim wait strands every non-chain mode and F27's arm is declared citable for nothing; and at the F28 gate car reads +6.6%, inside the band at a gate for the first time in the project - with ride still -42.8%, seven modes past the bar, and no run since F4 having reached the horizon it declared.

Build layer

A layered pipeline: OSM/GTFS/census -> tidy layers (A1..A6, D1) -> C1/C2 parameters -> B1 population -> B2 tours -> MATSim plans and run inputs. Every stage writes a `_*_report.json` beside its artefact and every path resolves through `src/city.py`. Three structural strengths: the config is BUILT from the registry rather than substituted into a template (`param_config.closure` refuses a leak), a value with a `derived_from` identity is checked at build time (build_activity_chains.py:1950), and two refusals actually fire (build_params.py:122, :171). Three structural weaknesses: the four binder passes each read and rewrite the whole 323 MB day file, the report a build writes is computed BEFORE those passes rewrite it, and the deepest decisions - a 0.5 stop-purpose split, a 0.02 education floor, a mobility-impairment curve, a weekday/weekend fallback shape - sit inside function bodies where the hardcoding ledger structurally cannot see them.

files 35 lines 16300 code lines 12629 functions 358 longest function src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:535 write_day, 742 lines, complexity 151, nesting 10 docstring coverage 0.509 todo count 0 functions over 150 lines 17 functions over 15 branches 49

Testability. Zero. No unit test imports any module of this area (code_metrics `tests.covered` = city, run_matsim, results_store, fit, outputs, param_config). The layer's own correctness is asserted by four build-time refusals (build_params.py:122/:128/:171, build_activity_chains.py:1950) and by the reports it writes, both of which only fire when the whole 2.3 GiB package is present. The pure functions that could be tested today with no data - main_mode-style folds, leg_purpose (build_activity_chains.py:867), income_band_midpoint (build_matsim_plans.py:424), tobler_factor (attach_gradient.py:62), kin (build_era1_reconstruction.py:73), leaf_mixed_tours (build_matsim_plans.py:495) - are exactly the ones that decide the plan file's shape, and none is exercised.

Run harness

One owner per concern, and the ownership is stated: `src/city.py` owns city paths, `results_store.py` owns run bytes, `run_matsim.py` owns run identity, `run.py` is a thin front door. Run identity is a parameter set plus three hashes (controler source, resolved registry values, population file), which is unusually strong - a rebuilt demand or a changed Java class refuses a resume. The three observers (live view, progress digest, gate watcher) are daemon threads that swallow every failure so instrumentation cannot kill a run. The weakness is at the boundaries between processes: `--stop` runs in a DIFFERENT process from the harness that owns the run, and the two race; `trim` runs on a daemon thread that can reach another run's directory; and liveness is judged on the harness pid alone though the card carries the JVM's.

files 11 lines 4101 code lines 3234 functions 141 longest function src/run/run_matsim.py:1126 run, 250 lines docstring coverage 0.601 todo count 0 functions over 150 lines 3 functions over 15 branches 9

Testability. The best-covered area, and still thin. Four checks and two unit-test files import run_matsim/results_store; the gate watcher and the launch refusal are genuinely exercised. What no test reaches: the --stop path (two processes), trim's interaction with a live run, reconcile_stale, the Windows Task Scheduler detach, bootstrap_toolchain (no test imports it), session_gate's arm classifier, and every one of the 66 committed run overlays - `phys_timing2_async_25pct.json` turns off the events-manager barrier that keeps RunTelemetry safe and nothing checks that pairing.

Analysis and calibration

Two layers with a rule between them: `src/analyse/` computes modelled quantities and is forbidden to open a target; `src/calibrate/` scores. The rule mostly holds - extract_metrics.py:436 says so explicitly - but four analysis modules do open the validation directory (report_mode_ridership.py:87/:126/:283/:294, map_count_stations.py:57), and one of them is the gate that stops runs. The gate path is the strongest piece of design in the area: the verdict is a FILE with an iteration number, the watcher refuses a verdict from another milestone, and a pass prints `GATE:` too so a substring test cannot kill a healthy arm (run_matsim.py:867-883). The weakest is the reader layer: nothing is cached, so the population LGA map (612,634 rows) and the transit schedule are re-parsed once per iteration reported, and output_trips is parsed four times in one extract_metrics run.

files 29 lines 10292 code lines 8668 functions 278 longest function src/analyse/report_mode_ridership.py:328 report, 278 lines docstring coverage 0.493 todo count 0 functions over 150 lines 6 functions over 15 branches 34

Testability. One module of 29 is unit-tested (fit.py, via tests/unit/test_fit.py). The gate watcher is tested from the harness side (tests/check_gate_watcher.py) with a canned reporter, which tests the watcher and not the reporter. Nothing tests the derivation the whole twelve-mode reading now rests on: iteration_trips.derive has a `--validate` mode that compares it against MATSim's own trips table, and that validation is a manual command, not a check in session_gate's list of 17. The two functions most worth a synthetic test - main_mode (iteration_trips.py:120) and leaf_mixed_tours (build_matsim_plans.py:495) - reimplement MATSim's own identifiers in Python and are the only place a divergence would show.

Contract and checks

The contract is unusually well built and the checks are unusually honest about being checks - check_hardcoding asks five separate questions because 'the answers mean different things', and check_city_agnostic states in its own docstring what it does and does not prove. The failure mode is uniform: every check is strong on the SHAPE of a declaration and blind to a value decided inside a function body. `extract_legacy_constants.scan_decisions` walks `tree.body` only and only ALL-CAPS names, so the ledger that 'is at 0 and stays at 0' cannot see any of the build layer's in-function constants; `check_city_agnostic` exercises the resolver and the emitter and never imports a build or analysis module, so a 'WEEKDAY' literal in the run-input assembler is invisible to the gate named 'city agnostic'; `check_legacy_drift` compares zero fields and passes.

files 25 lines 8758 code lines 6769 functions 311 longest function src/registry/render_docs.py:90 render, 171 lines docstring coverage 0.334 todo count 0 test files 14 test functions 95

Testability. The checks are the tests. 95 test functions across 14 files, of which 5 files are true unit tests (tests/unit/) importing 6 src modules; the rest are whole-artefact checks. What is NOT gated anywhere: the build layer (0 imports), 27 of 29 analysis modules, bootstrap_toolchain, prune_run, session_gate, and the Java except through six probes that need the signals run stack built. tests/check_package.py is local-only by design and needs the full 4.08 GiB package, so the strongest check in the repository does not run in CI - which is the right call and should be stated as a known gap rather than a property.

Acquisition and data

Acquisition is jurisdiction-specific by design and the split is respected: every adapter lives under the city, and the framework reaches its census/HTS/count vocabulary only through `reader_shapes.py`, resolved by `city.readers()`. The extents that were once typed rectangles are now DERIVED (overpass.py:69-77 from the dissolved LGA boundary, plus a declared margin) and the docstring records the 87-SA1 clip that made that necessary. The holdout is a pre-registered 67/143 split written into the target artefacts themselves. The failure is that the split is enforced at SCORING and not at DERIVATION: the heavy-vehicle share that converts 31 of the 34 calibration count targets to a light-vehicle basis is a median over 23 classified stations of which only 3 are calibration, and the truck GATE target is the pooled classified share with no split filter at all.

files 14 lines 2085 code lines 1692 functions 47 longest function cities/newcastle/extract/reader_shapes.py:250 residence_marginals, 62 lines docstring coverage 0.637 todo count 0 manifest rows 512 manifest raw rows 92

Testability. check_manifest.py (CI) verifies hash, size and licence presence over committed blobs; check_package.py (local, 4.08 GiB) verifies the rest. Neither can see a blank source, a blank retrieval date, or a target derived across the holdout boundary, because none of those is a shape a schema can express - they are joins between an artefact and the rule that produced it. The one test that would catch the heavy-share leak is a three-line assertion in check_package.py that C3's `stations_observed` equals its `calibration_stations_observed`; it does not exist.

MATSim extensions

MATSim core is unmodified; everything is an addition on the classpath beside the pinned shaded jar, with a second class directory for the signals stack that must never share a classpath with it. Extensions fall into four kinds: bindings that withhold a mode (AvailabilityModesCalculator, GatedSubtourModeChoice), engines that mutate the selected plan at BeforeMobsim and restore at AfterMobsim (RidePairingEngine, TaxiFleetEngine, RemodeRestore), event handlers that emit money (Parking, PtFare, Fare), and observers (RunTelemetry). The design discipline is real - six probes exercise the classes that decide correctness without a scenario, because the pinned toolchain carries no test framework and adding one would be a toolchain change. The exposure is concentrated in the second kind: an engine that writes into a selected plan between replanning and the mobsim is operating outside the sanctioned boundary, and the restore path has to find the same trip again by re-searching rather than by an ordinal it kept.

files 50 lines 14791 methods 617 longest method src/java/citysim/RidePairingEngine.java:490 notifyBeforeMobsim, 528 lines methods over 150 lines 7 system out calls 36 seeded random sites 1 unseeded random sites 0 string work near event handler 1

Testability. Six Java probes, run by src/run/run_signal_probes.py and by nothing in CI. They cover the signal assembly and physics, the SCATS and tram priority extensions, the shared re-mode restore, the mode-choice revert and the fare lookup - a genuinely good set for a toolchain with no test framework. Uncovered: every class that participates in the ride economy (RidePairingEngine 1,563 lines, JointRideEngine, TaxiFleetEngine, EscortCoherenceListener), the household vehicle roster and its new departure handler, RunTelemetry, and the whole of CitysimControler.assemble - the 502-line method that decides which of these are bound at all. A probe for the roster (a two-household toy scenario where the car is out) would cost a day and would exercise the newest and least-observed mechanism in the model.

findings

Ninety-five findings, ranked, each with a failure scenario

the sharpest five
  1. A measured holdout breach. The heavy-vehicle share that converts 31 of 34 calibration count targets is a median over 23 classified stations, 20 of which are holdout. The artefact prints its own contradiction: stations_observed 23, calibration_stations_observed 3. cities/newcastle/build/build_validation_targets.py:308-312
  2. The hardcoding gate is green on a rule it cannot see. The scanner behind values decided in code = 0 walks tree.body only and ALL-CAPS names only, so every in-function constant is structurally invisible to it. src/registry/extract_legacy_constants.py:135, :152
  3. --stop kills every concurrent arm and discards the operator's reason. run.py --stop A ends every citysim_run_* task; and the harness wakes before the stop path writes its record, marking failed and renaming the directory. No stopped_by_operator record has ever been written. run.py:212-220 · run_matsim.py:1102-1110 vs :1297-1300
  4. Counts are compared on two different bases. The modelled side sums vol_car alone against an observed light-vehicle basis, so motorbike, taxi and roster cars are counted against nothing and every count error is biased low — while #82 tracks counts at −91.8 %. src/analyse/extract_metrics.py:379 · fit.py:213-214
  5. The demand report counts legs before the binders rewrite them. It reports 2,189,888 weekday core legs against 2,225,838 on disk, and publishes a trip rate of 3.348 against the HTS 3.473 as a shortfall the file does not actually show. src/build/build_activity_chains.py:3174

optimisation ledger

Fifty-two candidate changes, sorted by what they would cost a result

The column that matters is the last but one. A change marked none leaves the output byte-identical. A change marked opens a family changes the demand, the network or the Java, so DECISIONS.md §3.5 makes the next arm incomparable with everything before it — such a change is never cheaper than the arm it invalidates. Rows are ordered accordingly: safe first, family-opening next, unknown last.

simulator performance

Where an iteration goes, and why 250 of them is no longer the problem

a correction to the collector, made this pass

stopwatch.csv nests `dump all plans` INSIDE `beforeMobsimListeners` (header columns 7-10: BEGIN beforeMobsimListeners / BEGIN dump all plans / END dump all plans / END beforeMobsimListeners), and the `dump all plans` duration column is EMPTY on every non-dump iteration.

Consequence. collect_performance.py:82-130 reports both as a share of `iteration`, so the phase shares of the F23 run sum to 1.187, and a `dump all plans` share is the share of a DUMP ITERATION while every other phase's median is over all iterations. F28's `dump all plans` share of 0.319 is 82.5 s on 3 of 101 iterations = 0.9 % of the run, not 32 %.

Threads saturate well before the cores do

threadsiterationof which mobsim
10272.0 s143.5 s
16268.5 s136.0 s
24270.5 s135.5 s

Going from 10 to 24 threads on a 24-core host buys eight per cent. The mobsim is not thread-bound, so the remaining headroom is not in parallelism.

Replanning, writing, and the JVM

At 25 % the model carries 154,347 agents and re-routes 36,244 plans an iteration in about 50 s on 20 threads. Innovation switches off at iteration 241 — all seven innovative slots go to zero weight — so the last tenth of a 250-iteration arm should be markedly cheaper. That tail has never been run: it is recorded here as unmeasured — needs an arm past iteration 240, not estimated.

Peak heap reached 37.7 GB against a 39.3 GB ceiling on the F28 stack, with a live set of 13.3 GB — above the compressed-oops boundary, which is why a -Xmx31g probe is on the ledger. Whether the heap was ever the binding constraint is unmeasured without -Xlog:gc.

the 250-iteration verdict

Reachable, and no longer the constraint. At the F28 arm's own measured median of 258.5 s an iteration (aborted_20260907T030352_300it_25pct, 25 %, 16 threads, 101 iterations timed, p90 282 s), 250 iterations is 64,625 s = 17.9 h of plain iterations; adding iteration 0, the two 100-interval milestones and the final iteration's forced events write puts a 250-iteration arm at roughly 18-19 h, and the innovation-off tail from iteration 200 - where all seven innovative strategy slots go to weight 0, removing 36,244 re-routed plans an iteration - should make the last fifty cheaper still, though that is projected from the measured composition and has never been run. Against the 27,657 s the same arm actually took to iteration 100, GOAL.md requirement 8's horizon fits inside a day on the machine as it stands, where the F23 stack would have needed 44 h. What would halve it is not available: the iteration is now 65.0 % mobsim, 19.3 % replanning and 13.2 % prepareForMobsim, our own listeners account for 0.8 %, and the mobsim is measured to saturate - 2.4x the threads bought 8 % (270-272 s at 10, 267 at 16, 264-265 at 24). Halving 258.5 s would need either a smaller fraction, which the 1 September directive forbids and §9.12 has already ruled unusable at 1 %, or physical work removed, which the twelve-mode goal forbids. The honest ceiling on further tuning is the 84 s in replanning plus prepareForMobsim that no timer decomposes, and the single untried lever that touches no result is the heap - 40 g against a 13.3 GiB post-collection live set, above the compressed-oops threshold, never probed. The real risk to requirement 8 is not the pace: it is that no arm has been allowed past iteration 100 in five consecutive families, so convergence itself, and the tail's own cost, remain unmeasured.

This is the widest gap between the project's ambition and its engineering. The gates are excellent — seventeen of them run at every session boundary, they are city-owned rather than hardcoded, and sixteen pass at HEAD. But they are almost all whole-artefact checks: they verify that the manifest matches the disk and that a document's numbers match their sources. Only six of 69 src/ modules are imported by any unit test, so the functions that actually decide the model — the binders, write_day, the gate reporter's measure() — have no test that could fail before a 22-hour arm does.

Of 56 test failures, 41 fall on a single branch (praneetdhoolia/f15-choice-set-seed-bound-ride) — a failure cluster on one lane, not a flaky suite.

the process finding of this pass

Every one of the 53 pull requests was merged with zero reviews. The convention that all work lands through a PR is followed perfectly — and it buys none of the thing a PR exists for. Combined with 63 of 69 modules having no unit test, the practical position is that no change in this repository has been checked by anything except its author and a set of whole-artefact gates. The gates are good, and they are not a reviewer: not one of the 34 defects in this report would have failed CI.

Median PR: +1,806 lines over 21 files in 4 commits; median gap between merges 0.12 days, longest quiet stretch 4.59 days. The Summary / Changes / Testing / Breaking-changes body shape arrives with PR #46 on 20 August and holds from there.

the commit log

Four hundred and forty-two commits, and six that predate the rule

442 commits between 2026-08-10 and 2026-09-07, 46 of them merges, by one author under two git identities. The message-prefix convention holds on 211 commits carrying a P<n> prefix; median subject length is 83 characters, and the longest is 482 — far past the ~72 the convention sets for titles, though that rule formally binds PR and issue titles rather than commit subjects.

direct commits to main

Six in the repository's history, and every one of them predates the rule that bans them. The last, ab1498f, landed at 12:04 on 21 August — seventeen minutes before PR #61 merged the ban at 12:21. In the seventeen days and twenty-five merged PRs since, there have been none. The root commit ba95e7a is the documented structural exception: a root cannot arrive by pull request.

All fifteen open issues carry the label — verified this pass — so the requirement is met mechanically. What the label means, though, is that fifteen known problems are each waiting on a measurement, and no run since F4 has produced one.

the structural fact of this project

Across 153 run directories and 369.5 machine hours, the highest iteration any run has ever reached is 100, and no run since family F4 on 21 August has executed the horizon it declared. That is not a failure of the machine — it is the GOAL.md loop working exactly as written: every arm is read at its 100-iteration gate, a mode is past the 20 % bar, and the arm is stopped so the cause can be fixed from the root. But it does mean requirement 8 — convergence within 250 iterations — has never been tested, and that eight of the twelve modes have never been observed anywhere near a converged state.

Eight of the ten are met or holding. The two that are not are the two that matter most: requirement 7, ridership within 10 % for every mode, stands at one of twelve; and requirement 8, convergence within 250 iterations, has never been measured. Requirement 9 passes its gate and leaks anyway — src/build/gtfs_tools.py:6 holds a typed Newcastle rectangle in the framework layer, which is precisely the failure mode the project's own constraint describes: a typed-in rectangle cannot be wrong in a way anyone notices.

the project in its field

Forty-one comparable projects, twelve platforms, and an empty rung

The field survey is a standing library, not a fresh sweep. All 40 stored project rows were inside their freshness horizons and were carried forward unchanged without a single re-search; the entire 39-search budget went to the library's two open gaps. That is what closed the platform lane, which had never delivered a row.

where this project sits

per-mode ridership, every simulated mode - ATTEMPTED, NOT ACHIEVED: the reading is from an aborted run at its iteration-100 gate and is not a result; one mode of twelve (car +6.6%) is inside 10%.

What the comparison says

  1. Twelve modes, each scored on its own basis, is the outlier: no surveyed project scores more than five or six. Berlin v6 runs car/ride/PT/bike/walk plus freight; AToM Melbourne four; the LA generative pipeline two. Nothing in the field attempts a per-mode reading of twelve.
  2. But 41 of 41 surveyed projects publish a fit and this one does not. Our scoreboard is a reading of an ABORTED run at its iteration-100 gate, which the project's own rule says is not a result; on that reading one mode of twelve (car, +6.6%) is inside 10% and seven are past the 20% stop bar.
  3. The rung we are aiming at is empty. Twenty of forty-one stop at road link counts, nine at survey shares, and only five - MATSim-NYC, CMAP, PSRC SoundCast, POLARIS Chicago, BEAM SF Bay - add transit ridership counts. Nobody sits on 'per-mode ridership, every simulated mode'.
  4. Berlin closes the gap we are hand-turning: an automated closed-form ASC update driven from survey shares converges in about five runs, and reports mode-share MAE under 0.5 percentage points on all five modes. We move ASCs family by family at ~22 h per 300-iteration arm.
  5. Sample fraction: 10% is the field's working default (Berlin ships 10%, 3% and 1%). We run 25%, which is what makes ferry and motorbike readable at all - and is also why an arm reaches its gate at 100 rather than its 300-iteration horizon.
  6. Signals are rarer in the research ABMs than the platform market suggests: Berlin states plainly that traffic lights are not modelled and calibrates free speeds instead. Explicit adaptive control is commercial ground (Aimsun Live, Vissim), which makes our SCATS-as-published-algorithm implementation unusual for an open scenario.
  7. The two things every platform has that we do not are a released, versioned artefact (MATSim 2026 Spring, 10 Apr 2026; ActivitySim v1.5.1; Aimsun Next 26.0.0) and other people running the same code - ActivitySim names fourteen member agencies, including Victoria's Department of Transport and Planning.
  8. The LLM-agent lane is the newest and the weakest on validation: every 2025-26 entrant scores distributional statistics (JSD, radius of gyration, trip-length distributions), and the field's own evaluation paper concludes the gap between narrative plausibility and empirical mobility realism is still substantial. Not one of them scores a mode against its observed ridership.

What others do best that this project lacks

whowhat they dowhy it matters here
MATSim Open BerlinAutomated ASC calibration: a closed-form update from survey shares that converges in ~5 runs, plus a three-way check against survey, routing-API speeds and count stations.Directly addresses the eight modes outside 10% without opening a comparability family.
ActivitySim / SANDAG ABM3An estimation mode that re-estimates model components on the local household travel survey rather than importing coefficients.Our behavioural parameters are declared and swept; none is estimated on the local HTS.
CMAP, PSRC SoundCast, MATSim-NYC, BEAM, POLARISTransit ridership counts as a routine, published validation target alongside link counts.We hold the target basis but have never published a fit against it from a completed run.
DeepCAM / DeepAM (Los Angeles)Household-COORDINATED activity generation - the household, not the person, is the scheduling unit.Our tours are per-person; the ride deficit (-42.8%) is exactly a household-coordination failure.
POLARISDemand and traffic flow in one discrete-event engine, so an iteration is cheap enough to reach a long horizon.Convergence within 250 iterations is still UNMEASURED here because no arm reaches its horizon.
BEAMWithin-day dynamic user equilibrium - agents re-decide inside the simulated day - and coupling to vehicle-energy and power-grid models.We replan only between iterations; the charging-dwell input is still a swept assumption.
mobiToppA seven-day activity horizon per agent, with actiTopp week schedules, plus a parcel/last-mile extension (logiTopp).We split the week into day types; weekly rhythm and CEP freight are outside the model.
Aimsun LiveA twin that runs LIVE against the operating network and publishes an operational outcome (Tees Valley: 14% delay reduction), not a fit statistic.Defines what 'digital twin' means to the agencies this work would be sold to.
SimMobilityAn explicit long / mid / short-term horizon split in one platform.Vehicle ownership and land use are inputs here, not endogenous choices.
eqasimA published, ready-to-run reproducible pipeline per city, released under a versioned tag.Our pipeline is as reproducible but has never been released as a versioned artefact anyone else can run.
PTV Visum 2026A synthetic population generator for activity-based models inside the commercial planning platform.The agency default is moving toward ABM; a twin that cannot exchange with Visum/Emme stays outside agency workflow.

BActivity generation and schedulingDaily travel budgets are strikingly stable: the Sydney Household Travel Survey reports an average 81 minutes travelling per person per day and 24-30 km per person per day across regions, with average travel time steady over the reporting series while mode composition moved (weekday train trips +3.1%, bus +2.4%, walk-only +2.7%, vehicle driver -0.8%, passenger -0.2%).literature: ~81 min/person/day travelling, 24-30 km/person/day (NSW HTActivitySim/CT-RAMP generate a full daily activity pattern per person from estimated models; MATSim takes chains as an input and mutates only times and modes during the run.INsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:289 (B.activity.act_duration_min), :251 (short-trip band), plus B.activity.hts_rate_per_person_day and B.activity.p_intermediate_stop / p_second_stop in cities/newcastle/registry/B_demaThe stable-time-budget finding is a check on the whole board rather than one mode: if modelled travel time per person departs from ~81 min/day the mode shares cannot all be right at once. A ~14% partially-joint tour share in the literature is the yardstick for whether the modelled bound-trip population (126,378 trips, seeded ride share 0.0451 at F29) is the right size before pairing is blamed.

CIntra-zonal tripsShort trips are systematically undercounted in travel surveys - the undercount concentrates on short walking, cycling and car trips for shopping and leisure, and every national survey from 1977 to 2022 has undercounted total walk trips by omitting short walks to stops and car parks. DDeparture-time profile by purposeDeparture time is a genuine choice, not a fixed profile: Small (1982) tied departure-time choice to a workplace constraint in the utility function, and travellers were willing to shift one to two minutes toward the early side, or one-third to one minute toward the late side, to save one minute of travel time.literature: willingness to shift 1-2 min early, or 1/3-1 min late, perActivitySim/CT-RAMP model tour departure-time choice by purpose; MATSim mutates departure times each iteration under TimeAllocationMutator and prices the result through the scoring function.INsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:314 (B.activity.departure_profile, six per-purpose 24-hour shapes) plus RUN.replanning.time_mutation_range_s -> timeAllocationMutator.mutationRange in cities/newcastle/registry/RUN_execPeak concentration decides how much of bus (+65.0%) and heavy_rail (+295.1%) rides in the peak, where capacity binds. A declared profile plus mutation is close to practice, so this is unlikely to be the root of either deviation.
DSchedule delay / activity duration preferencesThe schedule-delay cost function is asymmetric: the unit cost of arriving late exceeds the unit cost of arriving early, the disutility falls linearly to zero as arrival approaches the desired time, and Small hypothesises a FIXED penalty component on the late side - arriving late is always bad, however slightly.literature: late-arrival unit cost strictly greater than early; a fixeMATSim prices exactly this pair as scoring.lateArrival and scoring.earlyDeparture against an activity's typical and opening/closing times; ActivitySim carries it inside time-of-day choice utilities.PARTIALRUN.scoring.late_arrival_utils_per_h -> scoring.lateArrival and RUN.scoring.early_departure_utils_per_h -> scoring.earlyDeparture are bound in cities/newcastle/registry/RUN_execution.json, and C.scoring.activity_typical_Second order against the eight modes past the bar; it shapes the peak rather than the totals.

EAccess, egress, wait and transfer time weightsOut-of-vehicle time is valued well above in-vehicle time, and the multipliers are the best-established transferable numbers in the field. Wardman et al. report walk-time multipliers of 1.45 for urban and 1.70 for inter-urban trips and wait-time multipliers of 1.50 and 1.76 respectively; the 2026 update assembles 2,872 multipliers from 606 studies across 52 countries, 1963-2023, covering walk, wait, headway, displacemliterature: walk-time multiplier ~1.45 urban (1.70 inter-urban), wait-ActivitySim/CT-RAMP put these multipliers straight into the mode-choice utility; MATSim expresses them as the difference between a mode's marginalUtilityOfTraveling and the performing rate, plus utilityOfLineSwitch for tINC.time_weights.beta_walk_access / beta_walk_egress / beta_wait declared in cities/newcastle/registry/C_behaviour.json and translated at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1196-1197, where waiting_pt and utility_of_lineBus is +65.0% and heavy_rail +295.1% - both over-carry. If the declared access/wait weights sit below the ~1.45/1.50 literature central tendency, PT is cheap to reach in the model and that is exactly the direction of both errors. This is the highest-evidence, already-declared dia
EFares and money (income-scaled)Public transport demand is fare-inelastic in the short run and considerably more elastic in the long run: the recurring central tendencies are about -0.3 short run and -0.6 to -1.1 long run, with a meta-analysis reporting -0.24 short run against -1.1 long run and Schimek reporting -0.3/-0.7 across a large cross-section of US agencies.literature: short-run PT fare elasticity approximately -0.3 (range -0.ActivitySim/CT-RAMP carry fares as a cost term divided by an income-segmented VOT; MATSim prices fares through a money-event handler and one marginalUtilityOfMoney, optionally per person.INA.fare.* (the published Opal schedule, 40+ fields including bands, caps, transfer discount and peak windows) priced by src/java/citysim/PtFareChargeHandler.java, with per-person money sensitivity gated by C.income.represWith a short-run elasticity near -0.3, fares alone cannot close bus (+65.0%) or heavy_rail (+295.1%) - a fare change large enough to remove a 65% surplus is far outside anything observed. That is evidence the PT excess is a time-weight or access problem, not a fare problem.
EParking cost and search timeUnderpriced parking generates cruising, and cruising is a large share of central-area traffic: studies between 1927 and 2001 found 3.5-14 minutes to find a curb space and 8-74% of traffic cruising, with more recent work above 70%, and search time reaching up to 40% of total travel time. Shoup's operational rule is that a price producing roughly one vacancy in eight (a 12.5% vacancy rate) drives search time to zero.literature: 3.5-14 min search time in congested centres; 8-74% of centPTV Visum/Aimsun and MATSim's parking contribs simulate search explicitly against facility occupancy; ActivitySim prices parking as a cost term with a separate terminal-time component.INA.parking.search_min_max read at src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:940 with A.parking.search_time_representation='scoring'; A.parking.price_hr_max / price_threshold_pctile / charged_hours_by_day_type priced by src/javCar is +6.6% - already inside. Raising the parking cost or search time would push car down and the over-supplied modes (bus +65.0%, bike +157.3%, taxi +161.1%) further up, so this is a lever to leave alone until the eight modes past the bar are closed.

GIncidents and weatherWeather has a marginal effect on mode choice overall but a large one on cycling, and a smaller and less often significant one on walking: about a 4.0-4.4 K temperature rise, a 1 mm fall in precipitation, or a 7.1 m/s fall in wind gusts each corresponds to roughly a 10% change in cycling volume, and the effect is smaller in dense urban cores than in peripheral and rural areas. A perpetually fine day is a systematic upward bias on cycling of the order the literature quantifies, and it is one of only two mechanisms on this board (with habit) that bias bike in the direction of its actual error.
HUtility form (Charypar-Nagel scoring)MATSim's scoring is the Charypar-Nagel form: plan utility is the sum of activity utilities plus travel disutilities, with activity utility beta_dur * t_typ * ln(t_dur / t_0) - marginal utility of duration against a typical duration and a minimal duration below which utility is negative - and leg score built from a mode constant, a marginal disutility of travel duration, and a marginal disutility of distance. Under itliterature: activity utility is logarithmic in duration against a typiMATSim and its derivatives (eqasim, BEAM) score Charypar-Nagel; ActivitySim/CT-RAMP use nested-logit utilities instead, which is a different object - a nest coefficient has no MATSim equivalent.INC.scoring.performing_utils_per_h, marginal_utility_of_money, monetary_distance_rate, activity_typical_duration_s, activity_minimal_duration_s, mode_constant, marginal_utility_of_traveling, waiting_pt and utility_of_line_The form is what every deviation is expressed in. It is also the reason two well-evidenced factors cannot be carried: C.nesting.pt_coefficient (0.65) and the per-purpose VOT are both recorded as lost in translation (DECISIONS.md 9.3) because MATSim scores plans, not a nested logi

HLearning, replanning, plan memory, innovation switch-offThe distinction that governs convergence: while innovation is switched on - new routes, new times - the result is NOT truly stationary; if innovation is switched off the process is stationary but limited to the plans each agent holds at that moment. The plan set is the agent's choice set, and MATSim's recommended control is fractionOfIterationsToDisableInnovation rather than a per-strategy disable iteration.literature: no stationarity while innovation runs; stationarity after MATSim, eqasim and BEAM all use an innovation-off tail; ActivitySim has no equivalent because it does not iterate agents against each other in the same way.INRUN.replanning.max_agent_plan_memory -> replanning.maxAgentPlanMemorySize, RUN.replanning.fraction_to_disable_innovation -> replanning.fractionOfIterationsToDisableInnovation, RUN.replanning.weights -> replanning.strategThis is why no reading on the board is a result. Every arm since F4 stopped at an iteration-100 gate, before the innovation cutoff, so the deviations quoted are read from a process the literature says is not stationary. The 300-iteration arm design (cutoff at 240) is what makes t
HLLM-driven agentsThe 2025 evidence is that LLM agents can reproduce realistic travel behaviour and system-level dynamics in morning-commute settings and can serve as the agent model inside a multi-agent simulation such as MATSim; alignment techniques - few-shot learning and travel-behaviour persona loading - materially improve mode-choice accuracy and can surpass traditional discrete choice models where domain knowledge is supplied. literature: persona-aligned LLM agents match or exceed discrete choiceNo production city twin runs LLM agents; the work is research-stage, mostly as an agent model plugged into MATSim or as a standalone route-choice study.OUTno LLM or language-model path anywhere under src/ or src/java/; agents are scored by the Charypar-Nagel functionNothing on the current board, and the literature's own scaling caveat says it would not be feasible at 25% of a 500,000-person region. It is a horizon item, not a lever.
ITargets and the validation ladderPractice has explicit numeric acceptance criteria: transit validation standards of about +/-9% for regional estimated-over-observed boardings and +/-20% for transit screenlines, and MDOT screenline/cutline targets of 5% and 10% for percent difference between observed and estimated volumes. GOAL.md's every-mode-inside-10% bar is stricter than the FHWA +/-9% regional boardings standard applied to twelve modes individually rather than to a regional total - and the board honestly reports 1 of 12 inside.

IConvergence criterionConvergence in an iterative agent model has a precise meaning and a precise trap: the process is not stationary while innovation runs, and is stationary after switch-off only within the plans agents already hold. It has never fired, because no arm since F4 has reached its innovation cutoff - GOAL.md's 'convergence in <=250 iterations' requirement is therefore UNMEASURED, not unmet. IReplication across seeds / run-to-run noiseRandom seeds move agent-based results materially: across 100 seeds of one MATSim scenario, relative errors of up to 10% occur even on links with large volumes, and the variation between seeds largely dominates the variation between the two last iterations within a seed. Aggregate travel times are robust after one iteration, but disaggregate results needed about 31 simulations on average to reach a robust mean.literature: up to 10% relative link-volume error across seeds; ~31 repAimsun and Vissim require multiple seeded replications as standard practice; most published MATSim scenarios report a single seed, which is the field's most common methodological weakness.PARTIALE.replication.n_replications is declared (30, with a provisional planning figure of 5) and read at cities/newcastle/build/build_scenario_configs.py:40 and enforced by tests/check_package.py:117; RUN.machine.seed -> globaThis is the row that decides whether ANY deviation on the board is signal. JPopulation synthesisPopulation synthesis is the required input to any agent model because individual-level attributes for the whole population do not exist; the established techniques are iterative proportional fitting, iterative proportional updating, combinatorial optimisation, and Markov- and fitness-based synthesis. There is no clear guideline on choosing among them, and integer conversion and the zero-cell problem are the outstandiliterature: IPF/IPU/combinatorial optimisation/Markov the established ActivitySim ships PopulationSim; MATSim scenarios use eqasim's synthesiser or a bespoke one; every platform in the survey treats the synthetic population as an input rather than a modelled object.INsrc/build/build_population.py places households on SA1 residence marginals (:281) with age bands, measured licence rates (:62) and mobility-impairment and car-availability flags (:262), all under the master seed B.seed.mThe synthetic population's licence rates are measured rather than assumed (DECISIONS.md 9.131), which removes the usual first suspect for a car/ride misfit. Ride at -42.8% therefore has to be explained in the pairing layer, not in the population.
JTravel survey (HTS) weighting and vintageHousehold travel survey estimates are produced on a rolling basis from multiple pooled years and weighted to the ABS Estimated Resident Population for the collection year - so an HTS figure is a multi-year average, not a single-year observation. The survey's known systematic weakness is the undercount of short walk trips: every national survey from 1977 to 2022 has undercounted total walk trips by omitting short walkliterature: HTS estimates are rolling multi-year pooled and ERP-weightEvery activity-based model in the field calibrates against an HTS of this kind; the vintage-versus-base-year mismatch is universal and rarely stated.PARTIALB.activity.hts_rate_per_person_day and B.activity.day_purpose_mix are declared from the HTS and the mode-share targets are read through src/analyse/extract_metrics.py:8 against the published HTS MODE_SHARE definition, buWalk is -11.9% against a target the literature says is undercounted - so the true walk deficit is probably LARGER than the board reads. That strengthens the case that the walk and bike (+157.3%) errors are one substitution error at the short end, not two independent ones.
JSmartcard (Opal) and station countsSmartcard data is the standard calibration source for transit and it supports high-quality validation - agent-based models calibrated on it reach R-squared around 0.85 on on-board bus volumes - but it is structurally incomplete: most datasets capture only entry and egress points with no routing information, so trip-chaining is required to infer alighting stops and identify transfers.literature: smartcard-calibrated transit ABMs reach R^2 ~0.85 on on-boVisum, Emme and MATSim scenarios all calibrate PT to smartcard boardings where available; per-station validation for every mode is uncommon.INCAL.pt_split.window_months / station_scope / break_ratio / lr_observed_stop_share and CAL.pt.weekday_factor / censored_cell_value / censored_share_max declared in cities/newcastle/registry/CAL_calibration.json; B.opal.joHeavy rail at +295.1% is scored on boardings per weekday scaled by 1/fraction, i.e. exactly the smartcard basis. The literature's caveat matters here: an Opal tap is a boarding, not a linked journey, and B.opal.journey_linked is the declaration that decides which of the two the +
JRoad countsTraffic counts are not a fixed truth: counts alone vary by 10% or more from daily and seasonal variation, and FHWA recommends a minimum of one midweek 24-hour count at least every two years to obtain a typical ADT estimate. Validation percentages are therefore reported by functional class and against screenlines rather than link by link.literature: >=10% intrinsic variability in count data; validation repoEvery four-step and ABM practice validates on counts; MATSim scenarios in the literature report link-count scatter as the primary validation.INB.counts.heavy_vehicle_share and CAL.truck.count_year_from declared; src/analyse/map_count_stations.py matches count stations and cities/newcastle/params/C3_count_comparison.json holds the comparison - but src/calibrate/Counts are reported and not optimised against, which is the correct treatment given the external-tier bias. They constrain truck (level only, 5.96 against 15.47) more than any resident mode.

They put a floor under how precisely light rail (-45.6%) and heavy rail (+295.1%) can be attributed to any single change - a rebuild moves them for reasons unrelated to the model.
KSample fraction and scaling rulesDownscaling has measured limits: simulations at 25% or higher of the traveller population preserve all major urban traffic statistics, while below 10% even average statistics become unreliable, with scores and travel times the first to degrade. Rules that nothing enforces

Thirty-nine rules in .claude/CLAUDE.md were walked one by one. Thirteen are mechanically enforced, ten partially, and sixteen are advice only — including the ban on committing to main, the determinism and seeding rule, raw-download immutability, the ODbL/CC-BY lineage rule, one-build-per-comparison, and the PR title and body conventions. Several of these have held perfectly by discipline for 28 days; that is a fact about the operator, not about the repository.

published_docsREADME.md:373-379 states the boundary correctly ('OSM-derived layers are ODbL 1.0 share-alike; the rest CC-BY 4.0. Keep the distinction visible'), and .claude/CLAUDE.md carries the same rule. The rule is stated in prose and assigned by declaration; no check derives it from lineage, so a directory move silently relicenses a file.
the licence rule, half kept

Every one of the 512 manifest rows now carries a licence — the previous report's finding that 471 were blank is closed. But the same rule names three other columns, and they are not kept: source is present on 82 of 512 rows (16.0 %), retrieved on 59 (11.5 %), produced_by on 483 (94.3 %). And the boundary itself is assigned by five path globs, so 30 pt2matsim-mapped transitSchedule.xml.gz files are labelled CC-BY under scenarios/matsim/ while identical-lineage content is ODbL under networks/matsim/.

What the last report recommended, and what happened

Of the previous pass's twenty recommendations, the two that were acted on are the two that moved the performance picture: the ride-pairing cost was cut (recommendation 1's territory, though by a different route than proposed) and the iteration profile was re-measured. The remaining eighteen are re-derived independently by this pass and appear, re-ranked and re-evidenced, in the recommendations below.

appendix

How this report was made, and how to make it again

Reproducing it

Run /project-report in this repository. It executes three collectors and six agents, reads the standing reference library first, and writes exactly three things: this file, the row for it in docs/reports/README.md, and the refreshed library under docs/reports/reference/. It edits nothing under src/, cities/<city>/ or the living documents; it launches no run and recompiles nothing.

python .claude/skills/project-report/scripts/collect_metrics.py      <scratch>/metrics
python .claude/skills/project-report/scripts/collect_code_metrics.py <scratch>/metrics
python .claude/skills/project-report/scripts/collect_performance.py  <scratch>/metrics

Verification performed on this report

Ten cited file:lines were re-read by hand at HEAD and all ten matched: the holdout filter's absence, the AST scanner's two restrictions, the --stop kill order, the vol_car sum, the B2 report's leg count, the doc hook's gh pr create match, the position page's “459 fields” against 471 in the registry, the ride-pairing listener binding, run.py's task sweep, and _numeric_leaves' single level. Five sources searched this pass were re-fetched and all five held — ActivitySim v1.5.1, SUMO's EPL-2.0, MATSim 2026 (Spring) of 10 April 2026, and the PTV Visum row, which failed against its own FAQ page and was confirmed by its release note. Rows reused from the library were verified by inspection — a source URL and a last_verified inside horizon — and deliberately not re-fetched.

Colour and accessibility

The categorical palette was checked with the dataviz validator rather than by eye, in both themes: lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair separation under deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia, the normal-vision floor, and contrast against each theme's own surface. Both passed all six checks. Every chart carries a text alternative, hover detail on each mark, and a table of the same figures elsewhere in the document.
